Flap extension provides several advantages: greater lift for lower speeds, greater drag for steeper descent, increased forward visibility, and a reduced landing roll.

turns.content: Can you explain the phases of a normal approach and landing?
Certainly! A normal approach and landing are divided into five phases: the base leg, the final approach, the round out (flare), the touchdown, and the after-landing roll.

pairs.context: Normal approach and landing procedures are used when the engine power is available, the wind is light or the final approach is made directly into the wind, the final approach path has no obstacles, and the landing surface is firm and of ample length to gradually bring the airplane to a stop.

turns.content: I'm not sure when to start the round out during landing. Can you help?
The round out, or flare, begins as you approach the runway threshold and transition from descent to level flight just above the runway surface.

turns.content: I don't understand what the base leg even is or why it matters so much for landing.

The base leg is the part of the traffic pattern that connects the downwind leg to the final approach. Its placement is one of the most important judgments a pilot makes because it sets up the entire approach. You must accurately judge your height, distance from the runway's approach end, and rate of descent so you can achieve a stabilized approach, proper round out, and touchdown at your desired spot.

pairs.context: The placement of the base leg is one of the important judgments made by the pilot to set up for a good landing.

turns.content: I know the base leg distance from the runway depends on altitude, but what other factors affect where I should turn base?

Two additional factors affect base leg placement: current winds and the amount of wing flaps used. With a strong wind on final or when using flaps that produce a steep descent angle, you should position the base leg closer to the approach end of the runway than you would with normal winds or flap settings.

pairs.context: The placement of the base leg is one of the important judgments made by the pilot to set up for a good landing.

turns.content: On my checkride, the examiner asks: what airspeed target should I use on the base leg?

On the base leg you target approximately 1.4 times VSO, which is the stalling speed in the landing configuration. For example, if VSO is 60 knots, your target base leg airspeed would be 84 knots, calculated as 1.4 multiplied by 60.

pairs.context: The placement of the base leg is one of the important judgments made by the pilot to set up for a good landing.

turns.content: Why do we use 1.4 VSO specifically? Where does that number come from?

The handbook specifies 1.4 VSO as the target airspeed for the base leg because it provides an appropriate margin above the stalling speed in the landing configuration. VSO is the stall speed with landing gear and flaps in the landing position, and multiplying by 1.4 gives a safe approach speed. For instance, a 60-knot VSO yields a target of 84 knots.

pairs.context: The placement of the base leg is one of the important judgments made by the pilot to set up for a good landing.

turns.content: Should I deploy full flaps as soon as I turn onto the base leg?

No. Full flaps are not recommended until the final approach is established. On the base leg you should deploy landing flaps as recommended by the aircraft, but hold off on full flaps until you are on final.

pairs.context: The placement of the base leg is one of the important judgments made by the pilot to set up for a good landing.

turns.content: The examiner asks when I should complete the before-landing checklist relative to the base leg.

Normally, the landing gear should be extended and the before-landing check completed prior to reaching the base leg, not after turning onto it. This ensures you are fully configured and can focus on flying a stabilized descent once you are on base.

pairs.context: The placement of the base leg is one of the important judgments made by the pilot to set up for a good landing.

turns.content: What do I do with the throttle after I turn onto the base leg?

After turning onto the base leg, you start or continue the descent using reduced power while maintaining the target airspeed of approximately 1.4 VSO. Reducing power combined with the appropriate flap setting allows you to establish a controlled descent toward the runway.

pairs.context: The placement of the base leg is one of the important judgments made by the pilot to set up for a good landing.

turns.content: I get that there is usually a crosswind on base. How do I correct for it?

Because the final approach is normally made into the wind, there is usually a crosswind on the base leg. You must establish and maintain a drift correction by angling the airplane sufficiently into the wind to track a ground path perpendicular to the extension of the runway centerline, preventing drift away from your intended landing spot.

pairs.context: The placement of the base leg is one of the important judgments made by the pilot to set up for a good landing.

turns.content: Examiner question: what ground track should I maintain on the base leg?

On the base leg you should maintain a ground track perpendicular to the extension of the landing runway centerline. Because there is typically a crosswind on base, you angle the airplane into the wind enough to prevent drifting farther from the intended landing spot.

pairs.context: The placement of the base leg is one of the important judgments made by the pilot to set up for a good landing.

turns.content: If the wind is really strong on final, should I turn base farther out or closer in?

With a strong wind on final approach, you should position the base leg closer to the approach end of the runway. The strong headwind on final will slow your ground speed significantly, so a shorter base leg prevents you from overshooting or flying an excessively long final.

pairs.context: The placement of the base leg is one of the important judgments made by the pilot to set up for a good landing.

turns.content: Does using more flaps change where I should turn base?

Yes. When flaps are used to produce a steeper angle of descent, the base leg should be positioned closer to the approach end of the runway compared to a normal flap setting. More flap drag and a steeper descent path mean you cover less ground on final, so a shorter base compensates for that.

pairs.context: The placement of the base leg is one of the important judgments made by the pilot to set up for a good landing.

turns.content: What three things does the pilot need to judge accurately when placing the base leg?

According to the handbook, the pilot must accurately judge three things: height above the ground, distance from the approach end of the runway, and rate of descent. Getting all three right allows a stabilized approach, proper round out, and touchdown at the desired spot.

pairs.context: The placement of the base leg is one of the important judgments made by the pilot to set up for a good landing.

turns.content: My examiner asks me to explain the relationship between base leg placement and a stabilized approach.

Proper base leg placement directly enables a stabilized approach. By accurately judging height, distance from the runway's approach end, and rate of descent on the base leg, the pilot sets up the correct angle and airspeed so that the final approach, round out, and touchdown at the desired spot can all be accomplished in a controlled, stabilized manner.

pairs.context: The placement of the base leg is one of the important judgments made by the pilot to set up for a good landing.

The round out is a slow, smooth transition from normal approach attitude to landing attitude. It gradually rounds out the flightpath to one that is parallel to and a few inches above the runway. During the round out, airspeed is decreased to touchdown speed while lift is controlled so the airplane settles gently onto the landing surface, with proper landing attitude and touchdown speed attained simultaneously as the wheels contact the ground.

The rate of the round out depends on three things: the airplane's height above the ground, the rate of descent, and the pitch attitude. Since the round out is started at approximately the same height regardless of flap setting, the pitch attitude should be increased at a faster rate when full flaps are used, while still accounting for the airplane's downward motion.

That tail-down movement pivots the nose up, abruptly increasing the wing's angle of attack, which generates a sudden surge of lift and sends the airplane back into the air.

For a severe case, execute an immediate go-around with full power, directional control, and a safe climb attitude, again mirroring the response to a severe balloon.

turns.content: I keep hearing the term porpoising but I'm not sure what it actually means during a landing. Can you explain it?

Porpoising is a series of nose-first bounces that imitate the jumps and dives of a porpoise. It starts when the airplane touches down nose first instead of in the proper attitude, triggering repeated contacts with the runway. Each bounce can get worse if the pilot's control inputs are poorly timed.

pairs.context: In a bounced landing that is improperly recovered, the airplane comes in nose first, initiating a series of motions imitating the jumps and dives of a porpoise.

turns.content: I know porpoising starts with a bad bounce, but what are the root causes that lead to that nose-low contact in the first place?

Several factors can cause nose-low contact: inattention, not knowing where the ground is, mis-trimming, or forcing the airplane onto the runway. Ground effect also reduces elevator effectiveness and increases the effort needed to raise the nose, so insufficient elevator or stabilator trim can directly produce a nose-low touchdown that starts a porpoise.

pairs.context: In a bounced landing that is improperly recovered, the airplane comes in nose first, initiating a series of motions imitating the jumps and dives of a porpoise.

turns.content: On my checkride the examiner might ask how airspeed relates to porpoising. What should I say?

Excessive approach speed causes the airplane to float because it still wants to fly. When the pilot forces it onto the runway, a gust, runway bump, or slight control input can send it airborne again. That cycle of touching down and bouncing back up is how improper airspeed control leads to porpoising.

pairs.context: In a bounced landing that is improperly recovered, the airplane comes in nose first, initiating a series of motions imitating the jumps and dives of a porpoise.

turns.content: Why does ground effect make porpoising worse? I thought ground effect was supposed to help the airplane land smoothly.

Ground effect actually decreases elevator control effectiveness near the runway, which means more effort is required to raise the nose to the proper touchdown attitude. If the pilot does not have enough elevator or stabilator trim, the nose stays low at contact, and that nose-low attitude is what initiates the porpoise cycle.

turns.content: For a very slight porpoise with no extreme pitch change, what is the correct recovery technique?

For a slight porpoise with no extreme pitch attitude change, you can execute a follow-up landing. Apply sufficient power to cushion the next touchdown and smoothly adjust pitch to the proper touchdown attitude. This corrective action is the same as recovering from a minor bounce.

turns.content: What happens if a pilot tries to correct a severe porpoise using flight controls and power alone without going around?

When pilots attempt to correct a severe porpoise with flight control and power inputs, those inputs are often untimely and can increase the severity of each successive contact with the surface. These pilot-induced oscillations can lead to damage or collapse of the nose gear, making the situation more dangerous rather than better.

When porpoising is severe or appears to be getting worse, the safest procedure is an immediate go-around. Apply full power while simultaneously maintaining directional control and lowering the nose to a safe climb attitude. Do not attempt to salvage the landing with flight control inputs when the situation is deteriorating.

Severity is the deciding factor. A slight porpoise with no extreme pitch change allows a follow-up landing using power to cushion the next touchdown and smooth pitch correction. A severe porpoise or one that is getting worse requires an immediate go-around with full power, directional control, and a safe climb attitude, because attempting flight control corrections often worsens the oscillations.

The three elements of a go-around from a severe porpoise are: apply full power, maintain directional control, and lower the nose to a safe climb attitude. All three should be executed simultaneously and immediately when the porpoise is severe or worsening.

Yes, even minor disturbances can trigger porpoising when the approach is too fast and the airplane is being forced onto the runway while it still wants to fly. turns.content: What does it mean to force the airplane onto the runway, and why is that dangerous?

Forcing the airplane onto the runway means pushing it down before it is ready to land, typically when it still has enough speed to fly. This creates an improper nose-low attitude at touchdown. Combined with ground effect reducing elevator effectiveness, the airplane bounces back up, and the cycle of porpoising begins. Insufficient elevator or stabilator trim means the pilot cannot easily raise the nose to the proper touchdown attitude, especially since ground effect is already reducing elevator effectiveness near the runway. Proper trim before touchdown helps ensure the correct pitch attitude is achievable at the moment of contact.

During a severe porpoise, the airplane is oscillating rapidly. Each mistimed input adds energy to the oscillation rather than dampening it, increasing the severity of each successive runway contact and risking nose gear collapse.

Yes. A follow-up landing is appropriate only when the porpoise is very slight and there is no extreme change in pitch attitude. turns.content: I keep hearing the term wheelbarrowing but I'm not sure what it actually means or why it's dangerous.

Wheelbarrowing occurs when the airplane's weight becomes concentrated on the nose-wheel during the takeoff or landing roll. It's dangerous because braking action becomes ineffective and the airplane tends to swerve or pivot on the nose-wheel. This loss of directional control is especially hazardous in crosswind conditions where side forces can quickly cause the aircraft to depart the runway.

pairs.context: When a pilot permits the airplane weight to become concentrated about the nose-wheel during the takeoff or landing roll, a condition known as wheelbarrowing occurs.

turns.content: I know wheelbarrowing is bad, but what specifically causes it during the landing roll?

The most common cause during the landing roll is a simultaneous touchdown of the main gear and nose-wheel at excessive speed, followed by the pilot applying forward pressure on the elevator control. That forward pressure shifts weight onto the nose-wheel, concentrating it there and triggering the wheelbarrowing condition. Proper technique is to touch down at the correct speed and gently lower the nose-wheel as speed decreases during rollout.

pairs.context: When a pilot permits the airplane weight to become concentrated about the nose-wheel during the takeoff or landing roll, a condition known as wheelbarrowing occurs.

turns.content: On my checkride, the examiner might ask how to prevent wheelbarrowing. What's the correct answer?

Prevention comes down to three things: achieving and maintaining the correct landing attitude, touching down at the proper speed, and gently lowering the nose-wheel while losing speed on rollout. If you do those three things correctly, wheelbarrowing should not occur. The key is avoiding simultaneous main and nose-wheel touchdown at excessive speed and never applying forward elevator pressure during the landing roll.

pairs.context: When a pilot permits the airplane weight to become concentrated about the nose-wheel during the takeoff or landing roll, a condition known as wheelbarrowing occurs.

turns.content: If I notice wheelbarrowing happening during my landing roll, what should I do first?

The first corrective action is to smoothly apply back elevator pressure, which shifts weight off the nose-wheel and back onto the main gear. If runway length and other conditions permit, the handbook advises promptly initiating a go-around. If a go-around is not safe and directional control is lost, close the throttle and adjust pitch attitude smoothly but firmly to the proper landing attitude.

turns.content: When is a go-around the preferred response to wheelbarrowing versus staying on the ground?

A go-around is advisable when runway length and other conditions permit. However, if the pilot determines it is safer to remain on the ground rather than attempt a go-around after directional control is lost, the correct action is to close the throttle and smoothly but firmly adjust pitch attitude to the proper landing attitude. The decision depends on available runway and surrounding conditions at the time.

turns.content: Does wheelbarrowing only happen during landings, or can it occur during takeoff too?

Wheelbarrowing can occur during either the takeoff or landing roll. The handbook specifically states it happens when a pilot permits airplane weight to become concentrated about the nose-wheel during either phase. In both cases the result is the same: loss of directional control because braking is ineffective and the airplane tends to swerve or pivot on the nose-wheel.

turns.content: Why does wheelbarrowing make braking ineffective? I thought the brakes were on the main wheels.

That is exactly the point. The brakes are on the main wheels, so when weight shifts to the nose-wheel during wheelbarrowing, the main wheels carry very little load. With minimal weight on the main wheels, applying the brakes produces little stopping force. Additionally, the airplane tends to pivot or swerve around the nose-wheel, making directional control difficult, especially in crosswind conditions.

turns.content: My examiner asked why crosswind conditions make wheelbarrowing particularly hazardous. How should I answer?

In crosswind conditions, lateral forces are already acting on the aircraft during the ground roll. When wheelbarrowing occurs, the airplane tends to swerve or pivot on the nose-wheel, and those crosswind forces amplify that tendency. Because braking is also ineffective during wheelbarrowing, the pilot has reduced ability to counteract the swerving, making directional control loss more likely and more severe than in calm wind conditions.

turns.content: What is the correct landing attitude the handbook mentions for avoiding wheelbarrowing? I'm not clear on what that means in practice.

The handbook does not define the exact pitch angle but describes the correct landing attitude as the attitude that results in touching down at the proper speed with the main wheels contacting first. After touchdown, the nose-wheel is gently lowered as the aircraft decelerates during rollout rather than being pushed down with forward elevator pressure. Maintaining this attitude throughout the roll prevents weight from concentrating on the nose-wheel.

turns.content: I don't understand why a hard landing is such a big deal. The plane is only falling a few inches, right?

Even a small free fall creates significant force. A 6-inch free fall on landing is roughly equal to a 340 fpm vertical descent. When that descent stops within a fraction of a second, the load imposed at touchdown can be three or four times the actual weight of the airplane depending on the severity of contact. That kind of force can cause structural damage if the landing gear and other cushioning devices cannot absorb it properly.

pairs.context: When the airplane contacts the ground during landings, its vertical speed is instantly reduced to zero. Unless provisions are made to slow this vertical speed and cushion the impact of touchdown, the force of contact with the ground could cause structural damage to the airplane.

turns.content: So the landing gear is really the main thing absorbing the impact on touchdown, right?

The landing gear is the primary load-bearing structure, but it gets help. During the descent phase, the wings still provide some lift that aids in cushioning impact. However, as forward speed decreases after touchdown, lift drops rapidly. By the time vertical descent stops, lift is practically zero, leaving the landing gear alone to carry both the airplane's weight and the inertia force from the impact.

pairs.context: When the airplane contacts the ground during landings, its vertical speed is instantly reduced to zero. Unless provisions are made to slow this vertical speed and cushion the impact of touchdown, the force of contact with the ground could cause structural damage to the airplane.

turns.content: On my checkride, the examiner might ask what happens to lift after touchdown. What should I say?

You should explain that lift decreases rapidly as the airplane's forward speed is reduced after touchdown. At the moment vertical descent stops, lift is practically zero. This means the landing gear must then carry both the full weight of the airplane and the inertia force generated by stopping the vertical descent, which is why a hard touchdown significantly increases the structural load on the gear.

pairs.context: When the airplane contacts the ground during landings, its vertical speed is instantly reduced to zero. Unless provisions are made to slow this vertical speed and cushion the impact of touchdown, the force of contact with the ground could cause structural damage to the airplane.

turns.content: What exactly is vertical speed being reduced to zero at touchdown? I thought we were moving forward, not straight down.

During the landing flare and descent, the airplane has both forward speed and a vertical speed component, meaning it is descending at some rate toward the runway. At the instant the wheels contact the ground, that vertical component is instantly reduced to zero by the ground stopping the downward motion. The forward speed continues to decrease during the rollout. It is the sudden stopping of vertical speed that creates the impact force on the landing gear.

pairs.context: When the airplane contacts the ground during landings, its vertical speed is instantly reduced to zero. Unless provisions are made to slow this vertical speed and cushion the impact of touchdown, the force of contact with the ground could cause structural damage to the airplane.

turns.content: I know pneumatic tires help cushion landings, but what else does the airplane use to absorb impact?

The airplane uses pneumatic tires, shock absorbing landing gear, and other devices designed to cushion the impact. Together these systems increase the time over which the airplane's vertical descent is slowed to zero. Spreading that deceleration over a longer time reduces the peak force experienced by the airframe, which is critical to preventing structural damage.

A 6-inch free fall on landing is roughly equivalent to a 340 fpm descent rate. This comparison illustrates why even a small drop at touchdown generates substantial force. The airplane must decelerate from that rate of vertical descent to zero within a fraction of a second, and the landing gear along with residual wing lift must supply the counteracting force against the airplane's inertia and weight during that brief interval.

turns.content: Why does the load on the landing gear increase at the moment of touchdown instead of staying the same?

Before touchdown, wing lift is still partially supporting the airplane's weight, so the landing gear carries less than the full load. At the instant of touchdown, the vertical descent stops abruptly, adding an inertia force on top of the airplane's weight. Simultaneously, lift drops rapidly as forward speed decreases. The combination of the inertia force from stopping vertical descent and the loss of lift means the landing gear suddenly must carry a much greater load, potentially three or four times the airplane's actual weight in a hard landing.

turns.content: I understand the gear absorbs impact, but what is the role of inertia in a hard landing specifically?

Inertia is the tendency of the airplane to continue its downward motion. When the ground stops the vertical descent, the landing gear must supply a force large enough to counteract both the airplane's weight and its inertia. The harder the touchdown, the greater the inertia force that must be overcome in a very short time, which is why the load on the gear can reach three or four times the airplane's actual weight during a severe hard landing.

turns.content: If an examiner asks what the purpose of shock absorbing landing gear is, what is the precise answer from the handbook?

The purpose of shock absorbing landing gear, along with pneumatic tires and other devices, is to cushion the impact of touchdown and to increase the time in which the airplane's vertical descent is stopped. By extending the stopping time, these systems reduce the peak force on the airframe, preventing structural damage that could result from the sudden deceleration of vertical speed to zero.

turns.content: I keep hearing about inertia force and weight being separate things at landing. Can you clarify?

Weight is the constant downward force due to gravity acting on the airplane's mass. Inertia force is the additional force that arises because the airplane's mass resists the sudden change in vertical velocity at touchdown. When vertical descent stops instantly, the landing gear must counteract both the steady weight and this extra inertia force simultaneously. That is why the total load at touchdown can be several times the airplane's normal weight, especially in a hard landing.

turns.content: So after the vertical descent stops completely, what is the landing gear dealing with?

Once vertical descent stops, lift has decreased to practically zero because forward speed has dropped significantly. At that point the landing gear alone carries both the full weight of the airplane and the inertia force generated by stopping the vertical descent. This is the peak stress moment for the gear, and in a hard landing that combined load can easily be three or four times the airplane's actual weight.

turns.content: Why does landing while drifting sideways cause so much damage to the airplane?

When the airplane contacts the ground while moving sideways, the main wheel tire tread resists that sideward movement. This abruptly decelerates the sideward velocity, creating a moment around the main wheel that tends to overturn or tip the airplane. If severe enough, this side load can cause structural failure of the landing gear.

turns.content: I know hydroplaning is bad on wet runways, but can you break down the three types for me?

The AFH identifies three basic types of hydroplaning. Dynamic hydroplaning occurs when standing water, slush, or wet snow lifts the tire off the runway surface. Reverted rubber hydroplaning happens when a skidding tire generates enough heat to revert the rubber, creating a steam layer under the tire. Viscous hydroplaning occurs on a thin film of fluid where the tire cannot penetrate to the surface. All three can render the airplane partially or totally uncontrollable during any phase of the landing roll.

The AFH states that any one of the three types of hydroplaning can render the airplane partially or totally uncontrollable at any point during the landing roll, which means steering inputs and braking may have little to no effect.

Dynamic hydroplaning occurs when there is at least one-tenth of an inch of water on the runway. As airplane speed and water depth increase, the water builds up resistance to being displaced, forming a wedge beneath the tire. At a critical speed called Vp, the water pressure equals the weight of the airplane and the tire is literally lifted off the runway surface. At that point, braking action is nil and the tires no longer contribute to directional control.

turns.content: For my checkride, how do I calculate the minimum dynamic hydroplaning speed for a given tire pressure?

The formula is Vp equals 8.6 times the square root of the tire inflation pressure in PSI. For example, with a main tire pressure of 24 PSI, the square root of 24 is approximately 4.9, and 8.6 times 4.9 gives roughly 42 knots. That is the speed at which dynamic hydroplaning can begin. Remember, once hydroplaning starts it may persist to a significantly slower speed than the calculated onset speed.

turns.content: I keep seeing the term reverted rubber hydroplaning but I dont understand what makes it different from regular hydroplaning. Can you explain?

Reverted rubber hydroplaning, also called steam hydroplaning, is caused by a prolonged locked-wheel skid during heavy braking. The skidding generates enough heat to revert the tire rubber back to its original uncured state. That softened rubber seals against the runway, trapping water under the tire. The trapped water heats into steam, which lifts the tire off the surface. Regular dynamic hydroplaning is driven by speed and water depth, while reverted rubber is driven by heat from skidding and only requires a thin film of water.

turns.content: For my checkride, what should I know about how reverted rubber hydroplaning starts and what causes it?

Reverted rubber hydroplaning begins with heavy braking that produces a prolonged locked-wheel skid. The friction heat reverts the tire rubber to an uncured state, which then seals against the runway and traps water in the tire footprint area. That water converts to steam and supports the tire off the runway. Importantly, only a thin film of water is needed, and it frequently follows dynamic hydroplaning when the pilot keeps the brakes locked trying to slow the airplane.

turns.content: I know reverted rubber hydroplaning involves steam, but Im not totally clear on the sequence of events. Walk me through it.

Here is the sequence: first, heavy braking locks the wheels into a prolonged skid. The skidding generates heat that reverts the tire rubber to its original uncured state. That softened rubber acts as a seal between the tire and runway, preventing water from escaping the footprint area. The trapped water then heats and converts to steam, which physically supports the tire off the runway surface, eliminating braking effectiveness.

turns.content: How much water does the runway need for reverted rubber hydroplaning to happen? I thought you needed standing water.

You do not need standing water. Reverted rubber hydroplaning only requires a thin film of water on the runway. This makes it especially dangerous because a runway that appears nearly dry can still support this type of hydroplaning once a locked-wheel skid begins generating enough heat to revert the tire rubber and trap that thin film as steam.

turns.content: An examiner asks me what the correct recovery technique is for reverted rubber hydroplaning. What do I say?

The remedy is to release the brakes and allow the wheels to spin up, then apply moderate braking. Keeping the brakes locked prolongs the skid and sustains the hydroplaning condition. Releasing the brakes lets the tires regain contact and rotation, which breaks the steam seal and restores braking effectiveness.

turns.content: Why is reverted rubber hydroplaning described as insidious? That word is throwing me off.

It is called insidious because the pilot may not know when it begins. There is no clear warning that the tires have transitioned from a normal skid into reverted rubber hydroplaning. Additionally, it can persist to very slow groundspeeds of 20 knots or less, meaning the pilot might expect braking to work at low speed but still have no effectiveness, which can lead to a runway overrun.

turns.content: So reverted rubber hydroplaning often follows dynamic hydroplaning. Can you explain that connection?

Yes. During dynamic hydroplaning the airplane is moving fast and the tires are riding on a water wedge. The pilot may respond by locking the brakes to slow down. As the airplane decelerates below the dynamic hydroplaning speed, the tires begin to contact the runway surface but remain locked, creating a prolonged skid. That skid generates the heat needed to revert the rubber and initiate reverted rubber hydroplaning, so one type can transition directly into the other.

turns.content: At what groundspeed can reverted rubber hydroplaning finally stop being a factor?

According to the handbook, reverted rubber hydroplaning can persist to very slow groundspeeds of 20 knots or less. This is significant because pilots often assume that at low speeds braking will be effective, but this type of hydroplaning can continue well below what most would consider a dangerous speed, making it a persistent hazard during the landing roll.

turns.content: What exactly does it mean that the rubber reverts to its uncured state? Why does that matter?

Uncured rubber is the soft, unprocessed state of rubber before it is hardened during manufacturing. When skidding heat reverts the tire rubber back to that state, it becomes pliable enough to conform tightly to the runway surface and act as a seal. That seal traps water in the tire footprint area, preventing it from escaping. Without that seal, water would simply be pushed aside and the hydroplaning condition would not be sustained.

turns.content: Can you explain how viscous hydroplaning differs from dynamic hydroplaning?
Viscous hydroplaning occurs at lower speeds and involves a thin film of water, while dynamic hydroplaning requires higher speeds and thicker water layers.
